title: The London Baptist Confession of 1689 (Condensed)
subtitle: The Second London Baptist Confession (1689), faithfully condensed chapter by chapter, the great Reformed Baptist confession, with explanatory notes.
intro:
For most of the seventeenth century, English Baptists worshiped as outlaws. They were fined, jailed, and slandered, lumped together with violent radicals because they baptized believers and refused the state church. The confession bearing the date 1689 was actually drafted in 1677, in secret, and could only be published openly after the Act of Toleration. Its strategy was deliberate humility: the Baptists took the Westminster Confession of the Presbyterians and the Savoy Declaration of the Congregationalists and reproduced them almost word for word, departing only where conviction required: chiefly on baptism and the church. The message was plain. We are not sectarians. We hold the faith you hold. We simply hold it all the way down to the baptistry.

More than a hundred congregations signed it in 1689. It crossed the Atlantic as the Philadelphia Confession of 1742 and shaped Baptist life in America for two centuries. Charles Spurgeon republished it for his congregation in 1855. It remains the confessional standard of Reformed Baptist churches around the world.

What follows is a condensed summary of its thirty-two chapters, a faithful paraphrase, not the full text, which runs to many thousands of words and deserves unhurried reading. Even compressed, the order teaches: Scripture first, then God, then his decree and covenant, then Christ and salvation, then the church and the last things. The men who wrote it had buried friends who died in prison for these pages. We inherit them at no cost, which may be why we hold them so loosely.
text:
The following is a condensed summary of the Confession's thirty-two chapters. It is a faithful paraphrase, not the full text.

Chapter 1. Of the Holy Scriptures. The Holy Scripture is the only sufficient, certain, and infallible rule of all saving knowledge, faith, and obedience. The light of nature shows God's goodness and power but is not sufficient to give the knowledge necessary for salvation. The sixty-six books of the Old and New Testaments are given by inspiration of God; the Apocrypha is of no authority. Scripture's authority depends not on the testimony of any man or church but wholly upon God its author. The infallible rule of interpreting Scripture is Scripture itself, and the supreme judge in all religious controversies is the Holy Spirit speaking in the Scripture.

Chapter 2. Of God and of the Holy Trinity. The Lord our God is but one only living and true God, infinite in being and perfection, a most pure spirit, immutable, immense, eternal, almighty, most wise, most holy, most loving, gracious, and just. In this divine and infinite Being there are three subsistences — the Father, the Word or Son, and the Holy Spirit — of one substance, power, and eternity, each having the whole divine essence, yet the essence undivided.

Chapter 3. Of God's Decree. God hath decreed in himself, from all eternity, by the most wise and holy counsel of his own will, freely and unchangeably, all things whatsoever comes to pass; yet so that God is neither the author of sin nor does violence to the will of the creature. By his decree, and for the manifestation of his glory, some men and angels are predestinated to eternal life through Jesus Christ; others are left to act in their sin to their just condemnation.

Chapter 4. Of Creation. In the beginning it pleased God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit to create the world and all things therein in the space of six days, and all very good. He created man, male and female, after his own image, in knowledge, righteousness, and true holiness, with the law of God written in their hearts and power to fulfill it, yet subject to change.

Chapter 5. Of Divine Providence. God upholds, directs, disposes, and governs all creatures and things, from the greatest even to the least, by his most wise and holy providence, to the praise of the glory of his wisdom, power, justice, infinite goodness, and mercy.

Chapter 6. Of the Fall of Man, of Sin, and of the Punishment Thereof. Our first parents, by sinning in eating the forbidden fruit, fell from their original righteousness; the guilt of this sin was imputed, and corrupted nature conveyed, to all their posterity. From this original corruption we are utterly indisposed, disabled, and made opposite to all good, and wholly inclined to all evil.

Chapter 7. Of God's Covenant. The distance between God and the creature is so great that man could never have attained the reward of life but by God's voluntary condescension, which he hath been pleased to express by way of covenant. It pleased the Lord to make a covenant of grace, wherein he freely offers unto sinners life and salvation by Jesus Christ, requiring of them faith in him that they may be saved, and promising to give unto all those that are ordained unto eternal life his Holy Spirit to make them willing and able to believe.

Chapter 8. Of Christ the Mediator. It pleased God to choose and ordain the Lord Jesus, his only begotten Son, to be the Mediator between God and man — prophet, priest, and king, head and savior of the church, heir of all things, and judge of the world. The Son of God took upon him man's nature, so that two whole, perfect, and distinct natures were inseparably joined together in one person, without conversion, composition, or confusion. By his perfect obedience and sacrifice of himself, he hath fully satisfied the justice of God and purchased an everlasting inheritance for all those whom the Father hath given unto him.

Chapter 9. Of Free Will. Man, by his fall into a state of sin, hath wholly lost all ability of will to any spiritual good accompanying salvation. When God converts a sinner, he frees him from his natural bondage under sin and enables him freely to will and to do that which is spiritually good.

Chapter 10. Of Effectual Calling. Those whom God hath predestinated unto life he is pleased, in his appointed time, effectually to call by his Word and Spirit out of the state of sin and death into grace and salvation by Jesus Christ — enlightening their minds, taking away their heart of stone, renewing their wills, and drawing them to Jesus Christ; yet so as they come most freely, being made willing by his grace.

Chapter 11. Of Justification. Those whom God effectually calleth he also freely justifieth — not by infusing righteousness into them, but by pardoning their sins and by accounting and accepting their persons as righteous; not for anything wrought in them or done by them, but for Christ's sake alone; his obedience and satisfaction being imputed to them, and received by faith alone.

Chapter 12. Of Adoption. All those that are justified, God vouchsafed, in and for the sake of his only Son Jesus Christ, to make partakers of the grace of adoption, by which they are taken into the number and enjoy the liberties and privileges of the children of God.

Chapter 13. Of Sanctification. They who are united to Christ and effectually called are further sanctified, really and personally, through the same virtue, by his Word and Spirit dwelling in them. This sanctification is throughout the whole man, yet imperfect in this life; there abides still some remnant of corruption in every part, whence arises a continual and irreconcilable war.

Chapter 14. Of Saving Faith. The grace of faith, whereby the elect are enabled to believe to the saving of their souls, is the work of the Spirit of Christ in their hearts, ordinarily wrought by the ministry of the Word. The principal acts of saving faith have immediate relation to Christ — accepting, receiving, and resting upon him alone for justification, sanctification, and eternal life.

Chapter 15. Of Repentance unto Life and Salvation. Saving repentance is an evangelical grace whereby a person, being made sensible of the manifold evils of his sin, doth by faith in Christ humble himself for it with godly sorrow, detestation of it, and self-abhorrency, praying for pardon and strength of grace, with a purpose and endeavor to walk before God unto all well-pleasing in all things.

Chapter 16. Of Good Works. Good works are only such as God hath commanded in his Holy Word. They are the fruits and evidences of a true and lively faith, and cannot put away sin or merit eternal life; yet believers' good works, done in Christ, are accepted in him.

Chapter 17. Of the Perseverance of the Saints. Those whom God hath accepted in the Beloved, effectually called and sanctified by his Spirit, and given the precious faith of his elect, can neither totally nor finally fall from the state of grace, but shall certainly persevere therein to the end and be eternally saved.

Chapter 18. Of the Assurance of Grace and Salvation. Such as truly believe in the Lord Jesus and love him in sincerity may in this life be certainly assured that they are in the state of grace — an infallible assurance of faith founded on the blood and righteousness of Christ, the inward evidence of the graces of the Spirit, and the testimony of the Spirit of adoption.

Chapter 19. Of the Law of God. God gave to Adam a law of universal obedience written in his heart. The same law, delivered upon Mount Sinai in ten commandments, continues to be a perfect rule of righteousness. The moral law doth forever bind all, justified persons as well as others; Christ in the Gospel doth not dissolve but much strengthen this obligation.

Chapter 20. Of the Gospel and the Extent of the Grace Thereof. The covenant of grace being made known by the promise of the seed of the woman, the Gospel is the only outward means of revealing Christ and saving grace, and is, as such, abundantly sufficient thereunto.

Chapter 21. Of Christian Liberty and Liberty of Conscience. The liberty which Christ hath purchased for believers consists in freedom from the guilt of sin, the condemning wrath of God, and the curse of the law. God alone is Lord of the conscience, which he hath left free from the doctrines and commandments of men which are in anything contrary to his Word, or not contained in it.

Chapter 22. Of Religious Worship and the Sabbath Day. The acceptable way of worshiping the true God is instituted by himself and limited by his own revealed will, that he may not be worshiped according to the imaginations and devices of men. Religious worship is to be given to God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and to him alone. One day in seven is to be kept holy unto the Lord, which from the resurrection of Christ is the first day of the week, the Lord's day.

Chapter 23. Of Lawful Oaths and Vows. A lawful oath is a part of religious worship, wherein the person swearing in truth, righteousness, and judgment solemnly calleth God to witness what he sweareth.

Chapter 24. Of the Civil Magistrate. God, the supreme Lord and King of all the world, hath ordained civil magistrates to be under him, over the people, for his own glory and the public good. It is lawful for Christians to accept and execute the office of a magistrate; subjection in the Lord, and prayer for kings and all in authority, is a duty.

Chapter 25. Of Marriage. Marriage is to be between one man and one woman, ordained for the mutual help of husband and wife, for the increase of mankind with a legitimate issue, and for preventing of uncleanness.

Chapter 26. Of the Church. The catholic or universal church may be called invisible with respect to the internal work of the Spirit, and consists of the whole number of the elect. All persons throughout the world professing the faith of the Gospel, and obedience unto God by Christ according unto it, are and may be called visible saints, and of such ought all particular congregations to be constituted. To each church gathered according to Christ's mind, he hath given all power and authority needful for carrying on the order of worship and discipline. The officers appointed by Christ are bishops or elders, and deacons. Christ alone is the head of the church; the Pope of Rome cannot in any sense be head thereof.

Chapter 27. Of the Communion of Saints. All saints, united to Jesus Christ their head by his Spirit and faith, have fellowship in his graces, sufferings, death, resurrection, and glory, and are obliged to the performance of such duties, public and private, as conduce to their mutual good.

Chapter 28. Of Baptism and the Lord's Supper. Baptism and the Lord's Supper are ordinances of positive and sovereign institution, appointed by the Lord Jesus, the only lawgiver, to be continued in his church to the end of the world.

Chapter 29. Of Baptism. Baptism is an ordinance of the New Testament ordained by Jesus Christ, to be unto the party baptized a sign of his fellowship with Christ in his death and resurrection, of his being engrafted into him, of remission of sins, and of giving up unto God through Jesus Christ to live and walk in newness of life. Those who do actually profess repentance towards God and faith in and obedience to our Lord Jesus Christ are the only proper subjects of this ordinance. Immersion, or dipping of the person in water, is necessary to the due administration of this ordinance.

Chapter 30. Of the Lord's Supper. The Supper of the Lord Jesus was instituted by him to be observed in his churches unto the end of the world, for the perpetual remembrance and showing forth of the sacrifice of himself in his death, the confirmation of the faith of believers, their spiritual nourishment and growth in him, and a bond and pledge of their communion with him and with each other. Worthy receivers, inwardly by faith, really and indeed, yet not carnally and corporally, but spiritually receive and feed upon Christ crucified and all the benefits of his death.

Chapter 31. Of the State of Man after Death, and of the Resurrection of the Dead. The bodies of men after death return to dust, but their souls, which neither die nor sleep, immediately return to God who gave them. At the last day, all the dead shall be raised up with the selfsame bodies, and the bodies of the just, by the Spirit of Christ, shall be raised to honor and made conformable to his own glorious body.

Chapter 32. Of the Last Judgment. God hath appointed a day wherein he will judge the world in righteousness by Jesus Christ, when the wicked shall go into everlasting punishment, and the righteous into everlasting life, to receive that fullness of joy and glory with everlasting reward in the presence of the Lord.

annotations.phrase: the only sufficient, certain, and infallible rule
annotations.note: The Confession opens with Scripture rather than God, a deliberate choice inherited from Westminster. Before saying anything about God, it tells you how anything about God can be known. Method first, then doctrine.

annotations.phrase: neither the author of sin nor does violence to the will
annotations.note: Chapter 3 affirms exhaustive divine sovereignty and immediately fences it twice: God decrees all things, yet sin is never his work and human willing is never coerced. The Confession holds both ends of the rope and declines to explain the middle.

Covenant theology in one phrase: even unfallen Adam could not have claimed a reward from God by right. All relationship between Creator and creature is God stooping. Grace is not just the remedy for sin. It is the shape of everything.

annotations.phrase: not by infusing righteousness into them
annotations.note: Chapter 11 marks the precise line between Rome and the Reformation. Justification is not God making me righteous by degrees (infusion) but God counting Christ's righteousness as mine (imputation). One is a process I am inside. The other is a verdict I stand under.

annotations.phrase: can neither totally nor finally fall
annotations.note: Perseverance of the saints: not the claim that professing Christians never apostatize, but that those truly united to Christ are kept by God's power. The chapter grounds it in God's decree, Christ's intercession, and the Spirit's abiding, not in the believer's grip.

annotations.phrase: God alone is Lord of the conscience
annotations.note: The Baptists had been jailed under laws compelling conformity. This chapter is their scar tissue made doctrine. No human authority, church or state, may bind the conscience where God's Word has not. Religious liberty entered the modern world substantially through people who confessed this line.

annotations.phrase: limited by his own revealed will
annotations.note: The regulative principle of worship: God is to be worshiped only in ways he has appointed, not in whatever ways strike us as moving. A standing rebuke to every generation's confidence, including ours, that worship is a product to be designed.

annotations.phrase: the only proper subjects of this ordinance
annotations.note: Here is the Baptist distinctive, finally: chapter 29 of 32. Baptism belongs to those who actually profess repentance and faith, which excludes infants. The Confession agrees with Westminster on nearly everything and waits this long to differ, on purpose.

annotations.phrase: Immersion, or dipping of the person in water
annotations.note: Not a preference but, in the Confession's word, 'necessary,' because the sign must show what it signifies: burial and resurrection with Christ (Romans 6:4). The mode preaches.

annotations.phrase: really and indeed, yet not carnally and corporally
annotations.note: The 1689 view of the Supper is higher than many Baptists today assume. Believers 'really and indeed' feed on Christ, spiritually and by faith, not merely remember him. The memorial-only view common in modern Baptist life is thinner than the confession its churches descend from.
